text:
American philosophy - Wikipedia
Contents
American philosophy
American philosophy
is
philosophy
produced by
American people
, part of
American culture
. The
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
notes that while it lacks a "core of defining features, American Philosophy can nevertheless be seen as both reflecting and shaping collective American identity over the history of the nation".
[
1
]
The
Ivy League
colleges such as
Harvard
,
Yale
, and
Princeton
have long been influential in America.
Early American philosophy in the 17th and 18th centuries is largely seen as an extension of the
European Enlightenment
.
Colonial America
and the
American Enlightenment
was influenced by the
Puritan
thought of
Samuel Johnson
and
Jonathan Edwards
. The Enlightenment also influenced the philosophy of the
American Revolution
and
Founding Fathers
such as
Benjamin Franklin
and
Thomas Jefferson
.
A small number of 19th century philosophies are known as uniquely American in origin, namely
pragmatism
and
transcendentalism
, with their most prominent proponents being the philosophers
William James
and
Ralph Waldo Emerson
respectively.
American philosophy since the 20th century is mostly
analytic philosophy
.
[
a
]
Some of the most prominent American analytic philosophers are
W. V. O. Quine
and
Saul Kripke
.
17th century
While various
Indian tribes
(see
Indigenous American philosophy
) inhabited the territories that would later become the United States, most histories of the American philosophy have traditionally begun with
European colonization
, especially with the arrival of the
Puritans
in
New England
, such as those aboard the
Mayflower
who established
Plymouth Colony
.
[
3
]
[
b
]
Documents such as the
Mayflower Compact
(1620), the
Fundamental Orders of Connecticut
(1639) and the
Massachusetts Body of Liberties
(1641) served as foundations for the newly established settlements of the
American Colonies
.
[
3
]
These set the early colonial philosophy into a religious tradition (Puritan
Providentialism
), and emphasized the relationship between the individual and the community.
America's
first university
was
Harvard College
, established in
Massachusetts Bay Colony
in 1636.
[
4
]
The first 100 years or so of
college education in the American Colonies
were dominated by the Puritan theology of
William Ames
and "the
sixteenth-century
logical
methods of
Petrus Ramus
."
[
5
]
[
c
]
Massachusetts Bay Colony governor
John Winthrop
(1588–1649) emphasized the public life over the private. Others, such as
Rhode Island
co-founder
Roger Williams
(c. 1603–1683), held that
religious tolerance
was more integral than trying to achieve religious homogeneity in a community.
[
6
]
Minister
John Cotton
(1585–1652) influenced
Anne Hutchinson
(1591–1643), a participant in the
Antinomian
Controversy
which disrupted Massachusetts Bay Colony from 1636 to 1638.
[
7
]
Hutchinson was put on trial for preferring a
covenant of grace
to a
covenant of works
. With encouragement from Roger Williams, Hutchinson and supporters like
John Clarke
(1609–1676) and
William Coddington
(c 1601–1678) fled and established
Portsmouth, Rhode Island
.
[
8
]
Robert Calef
(1648–1719) wrote
More Wonders of the Invisible World
(1698) denouncing the recent
Salem witch trials
(1692–1693) and particularly the role played by
Cotton Mather
(1663–1728), who defended his actions in
Wonders of the Invisible World
(1693).
[
9
]
Mather was an early advocate of
smallpox
inoculation,
[
d
]
and deeply influenced by Sir
Isaac Newton
and
Newtonianism
.
[
10
]
Mather worked on a grand intellectual project he titled
Biblia Americana
, a commentary and interpretation of the
Bible
in light of "all of the Learning in the World".
[
11
]
Mather influenced
Benjamin Franklin
(1706–1790), particularly with his
Essays to Do Good
(1710).
[
12
]
[
13
]
18th century
Yale University was founded in
Connecticut
by a group of Harvard
alumni
,
Congregationalist
clergy in 1701.
[
14
]
The 18th century saw the introduction of
modern philosophy
,
natural philosophy
(or
science
), and the Enlightenment to colonial America. As a result,
Samuel Johnson
(1696–1772) and
Jonathan Edwards
(1703–1758) developed their own American theology and philosophy. "These two brilliant Yale students of those years, each of whom was to become a noted thinker and college president, exposed the fundamental nature of the problem" of the "incongruities between the old learning and the new."
[
15
]
Both Johnson and Edwards were originally ordained Congregationalist ministers. But Edwards based his reformed Puritan
theology
on
Calvinist
(or Reformed) doctrine, influencing the
Great Awakening
, while Johnson converted to the
Anglican episcopal religion
, and based his new
American Enlightenment
moral philosophy
on
natural religion
.
[
16
]
Both were used "in the tumultuous years of the 1750s and 1770s" to "forge a new intellectual culture for the United States",
[
17
]
which led to the Founding Fathers'
Revolutionary
political thought
,
[
1
]
and the subsequent
Declaration of Independence
(1776) and
Constitution
(1788).
Late in the century, the
Scottish Enlightenment
replaced these philosophies, remaining dominant up to the
Civil War
.
[
18
]
In 1714, a donation of 800 books from England, collected by
Colonial Agent
Jeremiah Dummer
, arrived at Yale.
[
19
]
They contained what became known as "The New Learning", including "the works of
Locke
,
Descartes
, Newton,
Boyle
, and
Shakespeare
",
[
19
]
and other Enlightenment era authors unknown to the tutors and graduates of Puritan Yale and Harvard.
They were first studied by Yale graduate student Samuel Johnson, who also read
Francis Bacon
's
Advancement of Learning
(1605).
[
20
]
Johnson wrote in his
Autobiography
, "All this was like a flood of day to his low state of mind" and that "he found himself like one at once emerging out of the glimmer of twilight into the full sunshine of open day."
[
21
]
He now considered what he had learned at Yale "nothing but the
scholastic
cobwebs of a few little English and
Dutch
systems that would hardly now be taken up in the street."
[
22
]
Johnson was appointed tutor at Yale in 1716, starting the American Enlightenment. Samuel Johnson has been called the "Founder of American Philosophy"
[
23
]
and the "first important philosopher in colonial America and author of the first philosophy textbook published there".
[
24
]
He was also interested in theories of education and knowledge classification schemes, which he used to write
encyclopedias
, develop
college curricula
, and create
library classification
systems.
[
25
]
Johnson believed "the essence of true religion is
morality
", and "the problem of
denominationalism
"
[
26
]
could be solved by teaching a
non-denominational
common moral philosophy acceptable to all religions. Johnson's moral philosophy was influenced by Descartes and Locke, but more directly by
William Wollaston
's
Religion of Nature Delineated
(1722), and the
subjective idealist
and
empiricist
Bishop of Cloyne
George Berkeley
, with whom Johnson studied while Berkeley was living in
Newport, Rhode Island
between 1729 and 1731.
[
27
]
Jonathan Edwards was "America's most important and original philosophical theologian."
[
28
]
Noted for his energetic sermons, such as "
Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God
" (1741), credited with starting the First Great Awakening, Edwards emphasized "the absolute sovereignty of God and the beauty of God's holiness."
[
28
]
Due to Harvard and Yale opposition to the Great Awakening,
New Light
Presbyterians
founded Princeton University.
[
29
]
Edwards was an associate of
George Whitefield
and a student of Samuel Johnson, who transmitted the influence of Bishop Berkeley. Edwards tried to unite a Christian
Platonism
with an empiricist
epistemology
, using the aid of John Locke's
Essay Concerning Human Understanding
(1690) and
Newtonian physics
.
[
30
]
For Edwards, there is an immaterial
mind
consisting of
understanding
and
will
, and it is understanding that leads to Edwards' fundamental notion of Resistance. Whatever features an object may have, it has these properties because the object resists. Resistance itself is the exertion of God's power, and it can be seen in
Newton's laws of motion
, where an object is "unwilling" to change its current state, whether in motion or at rest.
[
31
]
Though Edwards revised Puritan theology using Enlightenment ideas from Berkeley, Locke, and Newton, he remained a Reformed Christian and
hard determinist
believing in
predestination
. He rejected
freedom of the will
, believing we can do as we please, but we cannot please as we please.
[
32
]
According to Edwards, neither good works nor self-originating faith leads to salvation, but rather it is the unconditional grace of God which stands as the sole arbiter of human fortune.
[
33
]
Johnson strongly rejected Calvin's doctrine of predestination and believed that people were endowed with free will and
natural rights
. His original fusion of natural religion and idealism, which has been called "American Practical Idealism",
[
34
]
was developed as a series of college textbooks in seven editions between 1731 and 1754, such as
Elementa Philosophica
(1752). These works, and his dialogue
Raphael
, written at the time of the
Stamp Act crisis
(1765), includes sections on
economics
,
psychology
, the teaching of children, and
political philosophy
.
[
35
]
Elementa Philosophica
contains his moral philosophy,
[
36
]
which was promoted by President
Thomas Clap
of Yale, Benjamin Franklin and
Provost William Smith
at
The Academy and College of Philadelphia
(now the
University of Penn
), and taught at
King's College
(now
Columbia University
), which Johnson founded in 1754. These men "first created the idealistic moral philosophy of 'the pursuit of Happiness', and then taught it in American colleges to the generation of men who would become the Founding Fathers."
[
37
]
It was influential in its day: it has been estimated that about half of American college students between 1743 and 1776,
[
38
]
and over half of the men who contributed to the
Declaration of Independence
or debated it were connected to Johnson's American Practical Idealism moral philosophy.
[
39
]
In summary, "in the middle eighteenth century," it was "the collegians who studied" the ideas of the new learning and moral philosophy taught in the Colonial colleges who "created new documents of American nationhood."
[
40
]
[
e
]
The meaning of the term "philosophy" was not as narrowly circumscribed as it is today, and included science or natural philosophy, and the broad application of reason to
well-being
.
[
42
]
Back in Europe, publisher Benjamin Franklin was considered America's "first philosopher."
[
43
]
Franklin founded the
Junto
in 1727, and eventually the
American Philosophical Society
in 1743, with associates like
James Alexander
, botanist
John Bartram
,
William Coleman
,
Thomas Hopkinson
, and silversmith
Philip Syng
, creator of the
Syng inkstand
, used to sign the
Declaration of Independence
and the
United States Constitution
.
[
44
]
[
45
]
Newton critic
Cadwallader Colden
(1688–1776) joined a year later.
[
46
]
Franklin was known for his
aphorisms
found in works like
Poor Richard's Almanack
. Franklin's philosophical vision was broadly pragmatic. To quote him, "What signifies Philosophy that does not apply to some Use?"
[
42
]
In 1752, Franklin proved
lightning
and
electricity
were the same phenomenon with his famous
Kite experiment
, leading to the invention of the
lightning rod
.
[
f
]
About the time of the Stamp Act, interest rose in civil and
political philosophy
. Many of the Founding Fathers wrote extensively, including
John Adams
,
John Dickinson
, Benjamin Franklin,
Virginians
Thomas Jefferson
and
James Madison
, and Columbia graduates
Alexander Hamilton
and
John Jay
.
[
47
]
In continuing with the chief concerns of the Puritans in the 17th century, the Founding Fathers debated the interrelationship between God, the state, and the individual.
[
48
]
Resulting from this were the
Declaration of Independence
and the
United States Constitution
. Much of the debate surrounding the
Constitution
is found in the writings of Alexander Hamilton, John Jay, and James Madison published as
The
Federalist
Papers
.
[
49
]
John Locke's
Two Treatises of Government
(1689) was written to justify the
Glorious Revolution
(1688). It states government required the
consent of the governed
, and that an unjust ruler could be overthrown, thus providing a justification for resistance to
King George III
.
[
50
]
Thomas Jefferson (1743–1826) had been taught philosophy by
William Small
at the
South
's oldest university, the
College of William & Mary
.
[
4
]
[
g
]
Jefferson hung portraits of John Locke, Francis Bacon, and Isaac Newton at his home
Monticello
in
Charlottesville
, "the three greatest men the world has ever produced."
[
51
]
Jefferson penned the
Declaration of Independence
, altering Locke's
natural rights
of "life, liberty and property" to "
life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
."
[
52
]
Jeffersonianism
was a kind of
republican
agrarianism
. An alternative philosophy was found in Alexander Hamilton (1755–1804), whose
mercantilist
ideas formed Hamiltonianism or the
American School
.
[
53
]
[
54
]
The
Constitution
sets forth a
federal
and
republican
form of
government
that is marked by a
balance of powers
accompanied by a system of
checks and balances
between the three branches of government: a
judicial branch
, an
executive branch
led by the
President
, and a
legislative branch
composed of a
bicameral legislature
where the
House of Representatives
is the
lower house
and the
Senate
is the
upper house
.
[
55
]
This was influenced especially by
French philosopher
Baron de Montesquieu
's
The Spirit of Law
(1748).
[
56
]
Although the
Declaration of Independence
does contain references to the Creator, the God of Nature, Divine Providence, and the Supreme Judge of the World, the Founding Fathers were not exclusively Christians. Some professed personal concepts of
deism
, as was characteristic of other European Enlightenment thinkers, such as French philosophers
Voltaire
and
Rousseau
, or
French Revolutionary
Robespierre
.
[
57
]
They were at least influenced by Wollaston's natural religion, as evidenced by "the Laws of Nature, and Nature's God" and "the pursuit of Happiness" in the
Declaration
.
[
58
]
However, an investigation of 106 contributors to the
Declaration of Independence
found that only two men (Franklin and Jefferson), might be called quasi-deists or
non-denominational Christians
;
[
59
]
all the others were publicly members of denominational Christian churches. Even Franklin professed the need for a "public religion" and attended various churches.
[
60
]
Jefferson was vestryman at the evangelical Calvinistical Reformed Church of
Charlottesville
, a church Jefferson founded and named in 1777, illustrating the influence of Edwards reached even into Virginia.
[
61
]
Thomas Paine
(1737–1809), the English deist
intellectual
,
pamphleteer
, and
revolutionary
, wrote
Common Sense
(1776),
The American Crisis
, and
Rights of Man
(1791).
Common Sense
justified the Revolution and has been described as "the most incendiary and popular pamphlet of the entire revolutionary era".
[
62
]
Though popular in 1776, historian
Pauline Maier
cautions that, "Paine's influence was more modest than he claimed and than his more enthusiastic admirers assume."
[
63
]
Largely due to his advocacy for deism, Paine died in obscurity.
[
64
]
Boston Tea Party
organizer
Thomas Young
(1731–1777), who named the state of
Vermont
, was another revolutionary American deist, influencing
Ethan Allen
(1738–1789), leader of the
Green Mountain Boys
and author of
Reason, the Only Oracle of Man
(1785).
[
65
]
Elihu Palmer
(1764–1806) was also a deist.
[
66
]
The Scottish Enlightenment was introduced into American Colleges in 1768 by
John Witherspoon
(1723–1794), a
Scottish
immigrant and educator who was invited to be President of the College of New Jersey (now
Princeton University
).
[
67
]
He was a
Presbyterian
minister and a delegate who joined the
Continental Congress
just days before the
Declaration
was debated.
His outlook was based on the work of the Scottish
moral sense
theorist and
utilitarian
Francis Hutcheson
, who also influenced John Adams (1735–1826).
[
68
]
When President Witherspoon arrived at the College of New Jersey in 1768, he expanded its natural philosophy offerings, purged the Berkeley adherents from the faculty, including
Jonathan Edwards Jr.
(1745–1801), and taught his own Hutcheson-influenced form of Scottish moral philosophy.
[
69
]
John Adams's grandson was
Alexander Bryan Johnson
(1786–1867), whose
A Treatise on Language
(1836) anticipated analytic philosophy.
[
70
]
The Scottish-American
James Wilson
(1742–1798) was influenced by
Thomas Reid
's
common sense realism
and preferred Reid's justification for a people's right to rebel against an unjust ruler.
[
71
]
Wilson felt Reid had shown Locke's
representationalist
views led to
David Hume
's
skepticism
. Witherspoon's successor
Samuel Stanhope Smith
(1751–1819) was a dedicated follower of Reid and spread his ideas at Princeton.
[
72
]
Adam Smith
wrote the
Wealth of Nations
(1776), the classic statement of
laissez-faire
economics
.
[
73
]
[
h
]
Thomas Pownall
(1722–1805) anonymously published an essay for free trade titled
A Memorial Most Humbly Addressed to the Sovereigns of Europe
(1780), influenced by Smith.
[
75
]
Smith's
Theory of Moral Sentiments
(1759) was also influential, along with Hutcheson.
[
76
]
David Hume's physician
William Cullen
was a teacher of physicians
Benjamin Rush
(1746–1813), and
John Morgan
(1735–1789). Rush founded
Dickinson College
and Morgan founded the first medical school in America, at the
College of Philadelphia
.
[
77
]
Rush was a
materialist
,
[
78
]
as was oxygen discoverer
Joseph Priestley
, who had fled to America from Britain,
Thomas Cooper
, and Joseph Buchanan, father of
Joseph Rodes Buchanan
.
[
79
]
While not a strong influence at the time the
Declaration
was crafted,
[
80
]
[
81
]
[
i
]
afterwards, the ideas of the Scottish Enlightenment become an alternative to American Practical Idealism, and was the dominant moral philosophy in classrooms of American academia for almost 100 years, until the Civil War.
[
88
]
19th century
The 19th century saw the rise of
Romanticism
in America. The American incarnation of Romanticism was
transcendentalism
.
[
89
]
The 19th century also saw the rise of the school of pragmatism. Both are considered uniquely American.
The 19th century also saw the
War of 1812
and the
Civil War
.
[
90
]
Prior to the Civil War,
Andrew Jackson
's idea of
Jacksonian democracy
was influenced by Jefferson's philosophy.
[
91
]
Alexis de Tocqueville
published
Democracy in America
(1835), arguing a
democratic revolution
had taken place in America.
[
92
]
Jefferson influenced statesman
John C. Calhoun
, who led the
states' rights
and pro-slavery faction. Calhoun was one of the
Great Triumvirate
dominating American politics in the first half of the 19th century, along with
Henry Clay
and
Daniel Webster
.
[
93
]
The Civil War came soon after the
1860 election
of
Abraham Lincoln
.
[
94
]
Its aftermath saw the dissolution of the Southern
Confederacy
and the
abolition
of
slavery
.
[
95
]
American
transcendentalism
is marked by the
holistic
belief in an ideal spiritual state that 'transcends' the physical and
empirical
, and an emphasis on subjective experience. It can be viewed as a reaction against
modernism
,
intellectualism
, and
mechanistic
reductionism
. The transcendentalists all desired a deep return to
nature
. They believed genuine knowledge is intuitive and personal, and arises out of personal immersion and reflection in nature, not industrial progress and scientific advancement, nor the principles and prescriptions of traditional, organized religion.
[
96
]
Ralph Waldo Emerson
(1803–1882) wrote
Nature
(1836) and began the
Transcendental Club
, a conversational club of intellectuals, with fellow Harvard
Unitarians
influenced by
William Ellery Channing
, such as
Frederic Henry Hedge
,
George Putnam
, and
George Ripley
.
[
97
]
Several more intellectuals, both men and women, eventually joined, including
Amos Bronson Alcott
,
Orestes Brownson
,
Margaret Fuller
and
Theodore Parker
.
[
97
]
Margaret Fuller (1810–1850) was editor of
The Dial
, founded in 1840,
[
98
]
[
99
]
and translated
Johann Peter Eckermann
's book on German polymath
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
Conversations with Goethe
.
[
100
]
Influenced by Emerson, the Transcendental Club, and the importance of nature,
Charles Stearns Wheeler
(1816–1843) built a shanty at
Flints Pond
in 1836.
[
101
]
Considered the first transcendentalist outdoor living experiment, Wheeler used his shanty during his summer vacations from Harvard from 1836 to 1842.
[
101
]
Henry David Thoreau
(1817–1862) stayed at Wheeler's shanty for six weeks during the summer of 1837, and got the idea that he wanted to build his own cabin, later realized at
Walden Pond
in 1845.
[
101
]
Thoreau's book
Walden
(1854) shows his attempt to achieve transcendence through immersion in nature and the distancing of oneself from society.
[
102
]
Thoreau is also known for his essay "
Civil Disobedience
" (1849) which argues against compliance with
unjust laws
.
[
103
]
University of Vermont
president
James Marsh
(1790–1842), who introduced the writings of philosopher
Immanuel Kant
and
German idealism
to America,
[
j
]
was read by Emerson and the Transcendental Club.
[
106
]
[
107
]
Marsh influenced
William Greenough Thayer Shedd
(1820–1894), who combined transcendentalism with
High Calvinism
.
[
108
]
Marsh's cousin
George Perkins Marsh
(1801–1882) wrote
Man and Nature
(1864), which helped to launch the modern
conservation movement
.
[
109
]
The first systematic Kantian in America was
Laurens Perseus Hickok
(1798–1888).
[
110
]
Transcendentalism influenced a school of idealism and anti-materialism known as the
St. Louis
Hegelians
.
[
111
]
Their leaders
William Torrey Harris
(1835–1909) and
Henry Clay Brockmeyer
(1826–1906) published the
Journal of Speculative Philosophy
from 1867 to 1893, America's first secular, non-theological philosophy journal.
[
112
]
[
k
]
Personalism
is to be distinguished from Hegelian
absolute idealism
; it does not believe individual persons are absorbed into the absolute.
[
113
]
The founder of "personal idealism" or "California personalism" was St. Louis Hegelian
George Holmes Howison
(1834–1916).
[
114
]
"Personalism" simpliciter usually refers to the "Boston personalism," of
Borden Parker Bowne
(1847–1910), influenced by German philosopher
Hermann Lotze
.
[
115
]
[
116
]
[
117
]
Bowne influenced
Edgar S. Brightman
,
Ralph Tyler Flewelling
,
Francis John McConnell
, and
Georgia Harkness
.
[
118
]
Scottish-American
Thomas Davidson
(1840–1900) combined St. Louis Hegelianism with
Aristotelianism
, propounding "apeirotheism", which entailed each individual has the
potential
to be a God.
[
119
]
George Fitzhugh
(1806–1881) was a leading
pro-slavery
intellectual influenced by Scotsman
Thomas Carlyle
, who in
Sociology for the South
(1854) and
Cannibals All!
(1857) rebuked Benjamin Franklin, John Locke, Adam Smith, and the entire liberal tradition, preferring
feudalism
.
[
120
]
Albert Taylor Bledsoe
(1809–1877) wrote
Liberty and Slavery
(1856), "the most extensive philosophical treatment of slavery ever produced by a Southern academic".
[
121
]
Bledsoe is cited by
Lost Cause
advocates.
[
122
]
The
1848 Revolutions
brought more
German immigration to America
with the
Forty-eighters
, several of whom read philosophy and supported the
Union Army
. The most prominent was
Carl Schurz
(1829–1906).
[
123
]
Fritz Anneke
(1818–1872) was a
Marxist
revolutionary and Union Army officer.
[
124
]
Joseph Weydemeyer
(1818–1866) was a Marxist revolutionary and Union Army lieutenant colonel.
[
125
]
August Willich
(1810–1878) was a
communist
who served for the Union.
[
124
]
Pediatrician
Abraham Jacobi
(1830–1919) founded the
New York Communist Club
along with
Friedrich Sorge
(1828–1906).
[
126
]
The release of
Charles Darwin
's
evolutionary theory
in
On the Origin of Species
(1859) had a strong impact on American philosophy, including
John Fiske
(1842–1901) and
Chauncey Wright
(1830–1875).
[
127
]
They both wanted to understand
morality
and the
mind
in Darwinian terms, setting a precedent for
evolutionary psychology
and
evolutionary ethics
.
Evolution influenced
English
philosopher
Herbert Spencer
and American philosopher
William Graham Sumner
(1840–1910). Spencer coined the oft-misattributed "
survival of the fittest

Social Darwinism was also closely associated with belief in

and

Spencer influenced Sumner, a social Darwinist along with industrialists and

and

.

Sumner also advocated the
gold standard
. He further espoused
anti-imperialism
, coining the term "

". In 1876, Sumner became the first to teach a sociology course in the English-speaking world.

The most influential school of thought that is uniquely American is
pragmatism
. It began in the late nineteenth century, most notably with
Charles Sanders Peirce
,
William James
, and
John Dewey
, all of whom published articles in the
Journal of Speculative Philosophy.
[
112
]
Pragmatism begins with the idea that belief is that upon which one is willing to act. It holds that a proposition's meaning is the consequent form of conduct or practice that would be implied by accepting the proposition as true.
[
131
]
Harvard philosopher,
logician
, mathematician, scientist, and
polymath
Charles Sanders Peirce
(1839–1914) coined the term "pragmatism" in the 1870s.
[
132
]
The Metaphysical Club
included Peirce,
Chauncey Wright
, future
Supreme Court Justice
Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.
, and
William James
.
[
131
]
Peirce was a chemist and surveyor, who read Kant, as well as British philosopher
Richard Whately
. Whately started a revival in logic with his
Elements of Logic
(1826), in reaction to the anti-logical aspects of British empiricism. As a logician, Peirce was notable for pioneering the logic of
relations
(or relatives) and conceiving of
logic gates
.
[
m
]
Peirce's philosophy
includes a pervasive
three-category system
, combining a "
critical common-sensism
" (Scottish common sense realism plus
fallibilism
), with logic (including
Peirce's
semiotics
,
modes of inference
, and
methods of inquiry
), as well as
scholastic realism
for
universals
, Christianity,
objective idealism
influenced by Kant, and belief in the reality of
continuity
,
chance
, mechanical necessity, and
creative love
as principles operative in the cosmos.
[
134
]
In addition to making significant contributions to logic, semiotics (or the study of
signs
), and mathematics, Peirce wrote the founding documents of pragmatism, "
The Fixation of Belief
" (1877) and
"How to Make Our Ideas Clear"
(1878). In 1879, Peirce was appointed logic lecturer at
Johns Hopkins University
in
Baltimore, Maryland
.
[
134
]
In "The Fixation of Belief" Peirce argues for the superiority of the
scientific method
in settling belief on theoretical questions. In "How to Make Our Ideas Clear", Peirce harkens back to Descartes' notion of "clear and distinct ideas", and sums up pragmatism by what he called the
pragmatic maxim
: "Consider what effects, that might conceivably have practical bearings, we conceive the object of our conception to have. Then, our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object". The theory is that the meaning of a concept is equivalent to its practical implications, as a method of experimentational mental
reflection
.
[
135
]
Peirce coined the notion of
abduction
as distinct from
induction
and
deduction
.
In semiotics, the first two major theories are those of Peirce and Swiss theorist
Ferdinand de Saussure
.
[
136
]
As a mathematician, Peirce was a
founder of statistics
.
C. I. Lewis
wrote, "The contributions of C. S. Peirce to symbolic logic are more numerous and varied than those of any other writer—at least in the nineteenth century."
Paul Weiss
wrote Peirce was "the most original and versatile of America's philosophers and America's greatest logician".
[
137
]
British philosopher
Bertrand Russell
wrote Peirce "was one of the most original minds of the later nineteenth century and certainly the greatest American thinker ever".

James is best known as the author of
The Varieties of Religious Experience
(1902), his monumental tome
The Principles of Psychology
(1890), and his lecture "
The Will to Believe
" (1896). James, along with Peirce,
[
142
]
saw pragmatism as embodying familiar attitudes, elaborated into a radical, new philosophical method of clarifying ideas and resolving dilemmas. In
Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking
(1910), James paraphrased Peirce's pragmatic maxim as follows:
[T]he tangible fact at the root of all our thought-distinctions, however subtle, is that there is no one of them so fine as to consist in anything but a possible difference of practice. To attain perfect clearness in our thoughts of an object, then, we need only consider what conceivable effects of a practical kind the object may involve — what sensations we are to expect from it, and what reactions we must prepare.
